title: Ploughing
note: Ploughing belongs mostly to the cultivators’ varna and a little to merchants, and others may have it done for them. It is the effort that raises a family, so it follows that chapter.

couplets.plain: The world may turn every way, but it still follows the plough. So for all its toil, ploughing comes first.
couplets.pm: People avoid the bodily strain of ploughing and go round doing other work, but in the end the world follows those with the plough. Even with money from other work, they must go to the ploughman for food. So for all its pain ploughing is the foremost work, and other work, painless as it may be, is the lowest.

links.quote: for all its toil, ploughing comes first
links.reason: For all its toil, ploughing is ranked first among the ways of earning a living.

couplets.plain: Those who plough are the linchpin of the world, because they carry all who can’t and go off to other work.
couplets.pm: Those able to plough are the linchpin of the chariot that is the rest of the world, because they bear all who can’t do it and go to other work. This includes those who have others plough for them. Some read it that those who can’t plough bear every insult from their patrons and can only bow to them.

links.quote: they carry all who can’t and go off to other work
Those who plough are the linchpin of the world
links.reason: Speaks of those who plough by name and of the place they hold in the world.
The world is a cart, and those who plough the small pin that keeps it together.

couplets.plain: Only those who plough and eat really live. All the rest bow to eat, and walk behind others.
couplets.pm: Those who plough so that everyone can eat, and eat from it themselves, are the only ones who live as their own masters. All the others bow to someone and eat by that. People born human like anyone, who worship others, keep alive on the little they are given and walk behind them, don’t belong to themselves.

links.quote: All the rest bow to eat
Only those who plough and eat really live

couplets.plain: Those who have the shade of ripe grain will see the shade of many royal parasols come under their own.
couplets.pm: Those with grain from ploughing, whose kindness is like shade, will see the whole earth, now under the parasols of many rulers, come under the parasol of their own ruler. Their grain feeds all who ask and swells his power, so that all the land becomes his. “Their own parasol” is his, because they are one with him.

links.reason: Ripe grain brings the parasols of many rulers under the farmers’ own.

couplets.plain: Those who by nature eat by the work of their own hands won’t beg. They give to those who beg, and hide nothing.
couplets.pm: Those whose nature is to plough with their own hands and eat don’t beg from others. They give those who beg from them whatever they ask, and hide nothing. Living this way means they have wealth that never runs out.

links.reason: Living by your own hands frees you from asking and leaves you able to give.

links.quote: eat by the work of their own hands
links.reason: Describes those who eat by the work of their own hands.

couplets.plain: If those who plough fold their hands, even those who say they have given up all desire can’t stand firm.
couplets.pm: If the hands of those who plough fold and stop, the food everyone wants won’t exist, and those who say they have renounced can’t stay in that righteousness. If those hands alone lie idle, the world loses this life, the next and liberation. Some read “those who say they have given up desire itself”.

links.quote: even those who say they have given up all desire can’t stand firm
If those who plough fold their hands
links.reason: Everything turns on the hands of those who plough: what happens if they fold them.

couplets.plain: Let the ploughed earth dry until it weighs a quarter of what it did, and the crop will thrive with not a handful of manure.
couplets.pm: If a man who has ploughed his land lets it dry until a measure of its dust weighs only a quarter of that, the crop he plants there will need not even a handful of manure and will grow thick.

links.quote: the crop will thrive with not a handful of manure

couplets.plain: Manuring does more good than ploughing. After weeding, guarding the crop does more good than watering.
couplets.pm: For the crop, manuring is better than ploughing. Once these are done and it is weeded, guarding it is better than running water to it. Guarding means keeping cattle and the like from ruining it. Five things are needed in this order: ploughing, manuring, weeding, watering and guarding.

couplets.plain: If the owner doesn’t go to it and just stays put, the land will resent it and sulk like a wife.
couplets.pm: If the land’s owner sits idle and doesn’t go there daily to see to it, the land turns sour inside, as his wife would, and then sulks with him. “Owner” shows he must go himself and not just send others. A wife sulks when he stays elsewhere and doesn’t come to her, and he loses his pleasure.

links.quote: doesn’t go to it and just stays put
links.reason: Staying put instead of going out to the land is the neglect the land resents.

links.quote: If the owner doesn’t go to it
links.reason: A word to the owner who leaves his fields unvisited.
Gives the ground a wife’s sulk at being left alone.

couplets.plain: When she sees people sitting idle, saying, “We have nothing,” the good woman called earth laughs.
couplets.pm: When she sees people who say, “We are poor,” and sit idle, the good lady called earth laughs to herself. She is good because she gives wealth to all who plough. She laughs at the folly of seeing that and staying poor. Some read “those who beg”. This also leads to the next chapter.
couplets.sensitive: mocks those who say they have nothing to eat

links.reason: Laughs at the idle who say they have nothing, since the ground was there to be worked.

links.quote: the good woman called earth laughs

ideaLinks.quote: They give to those who beg, and hide nothing
ideaLinks.reason: Eating by the work of your own hands leaves you able to give to all who beg.

ideaLinks.quote: even those who say they have given up all desire
ideaLinks.reason: Even those who have given up all desire can’t stand firm once those who plough fold their hands.
